# Detecting supramolecular organic nanoparticles during heat wave

**Authors:** Renyi Zhang; Yixin Li; Jiayun Zhao; Bianca Aridjis-Olivos; Lijun Zhao; Veronica Kowalewski; Maisha Kabir; Natalie M. Johnson; Erik R. Nielsen; Sarah D. Brooks; Yue Zhang; Arnold Vedlitz; Weston Porter; Simon W. North; Wanhe Li; Michael W. Young; John H. Seinfeld; Yuhan Wang; Yuan Wang

## Abstract

Understanding how aerosols are formed is one of the foremost frontiers in atmospheric research, with profound implications for human and ecosystem health, weather, and climate. As the major contributor to fine aerosols, new particle formation produces >50% of cloud condensation nuclei in the troposphere. Aerosol nucleation is typically described by a two-step process involving a free energy barrier (e.g., nonspontaneous) and a curvature barrier (e.g., volatility-limited). Various chemical species—such as sulfuric acid, ammonia and amines, and oxidized organics—have been proposed to explain its occurrence. Climate change is expected to alter emissions and atmospheric chemistry, thereby affecting the frequency and nature of aerosol formation.

Available experimental, field, and theoretical studies often yield conflicting results, particularly concerning the chemical species responsible for the initial stages of aerosol formation. Owing to the lack of analytical instruments, direct measurements of the chemical composition of sub-10-nm particles remain scarce. To remedy these gaps, we conducted field observations and quantum chemical calculations to elucidate atmospheric chemistry under heat wave conditions. The size-resolved chemical composition of nanoparticles as small as 3 nm was measured, providing mechanistic insights into their formation and growth.

We observed frequent new particle formation at high temperatures approaching 40°C. Multifunctional carboxylic acids (e.g., diacids and triacids) were identified as the dominant constituents of nucleation-mode particles (3 to 25 nm), whereas the mass fraction of sulfuric acid increased with size. Amines were detected only in larger particles (>20 nm). We also found that the mass fraction of nonacidic organics, including oligomeric products formed from heterogeneous reactions, increased with size. Nucleation-mode particles exhibited distinct physicochemical properties, notably, low hygroscopicity and density characteristic of their distinctive nanostructures. Detection of gaseous organic acids confirmed their critical role in new particle formation and their origins from photooxidation of anthropogenic and biogenic emissions, such as traffic-related aromatics and biogenic-related isoprene and pinenes. Theoretical calculations showed that diacids and triacids, which have multiple branches for growth and stabilization, readily engage in double-hydrogen-bond formation to yield supramolecular nanoparticles—a process that is jointly augmented by dipole-dipole interaction and electrostatic attraction.

An unexpected finding from our field observations is the high temperatures at which frequent new particle formation takes place. Such a result cannot be explained by existing theories, especially those involving volatility-based nucleation. In contrast, our work uncovers a spontaneous mechanism in which supramolecular nanoparticles are produced from self-assembly of carboxylic acids through hydrogen-bond interactions. Revelation of the chemical identity of nanoparticles down to 3 nm provides the definitive evidence that multifunctional organic acids contribute dominantly to the formation of nucleation-mode particles. Given that organic acids are ubiquitously produced from photooxidation of anthropogenic and biogenic volatile organic compounds, their molecular self-assembly—in conjunction with sulfuric acid—represents a widespread pathway for new particle formation. Our study not only opens new avenues for assessing the impacts of aerosols on public health, cloud formation, and climate but also has broader implications for many biological, chemical, engineering, medical, and physical disciplines.

## Abstract

Supramolecular nanoparticles in air. Volatile organic compounds are emitted from anthropogenic (e.g., aromatics from traffic) and biogenic (e.g., isoprene from oak trees and pinenes from pine trees) sources. Under intense solar radiation, their oxidation by hydroxyl radicals produces large quantities of organic acids, which undergo self-assembly to form supramolecular nanoparticles. These nanoparticles are prevalent during heat waves, a phenomenon likely to become more frequent in a warming climate.

## Abstract

New particle formation (NPF) represents a major source of tropospheric fine aerosols. A common viewpoint is that NPF hinges thermodynamically on the volatility of condensing species and is unfavorable at high temperatures. From an intensive field campaign, we observed frequent NPF events during a heat wave. Size-resolved chemical composition of nanoparticles down to 3 nanometers was first measured, unraveling a dominant presence of carboxylic acids. Our work uncovers a spontaneous mechanism to produce supramolecular nanoparticles through self-assembly of organic acids. This discovery explains not only the unexpected NPF at high temperatures but also its ubiquitous occurrence under diverse atmospheric conditions. As global warming leads to more frequent and intense heat waves, our findings open avenues for assessing the impacts of aerosols on cloud formation, public health, and climate.

As the key components in regulating Earth’s energy budget, aerosol-radiation and aerosol-cloud interactions not only produce the largest cooling effect but also are the most uncertain in the projection for future climate (1, 2). In addition, human exposure to fine aerosols corresponds to the fifth-ranking risk factor for global mortality, resulting in >7 million premature deaths annually (3, 4). A large fraction of the tropospheric aerosol burden is generated from gas-to-particle conversion, which involves a multitude of complex chemical processes such as gas-phase photooxidation and new particle formation (NPF) (5, 6). In particular, NPF is responsible for a large fraction of cloud condensation nuclei (>50%) under various environmental conditions (7–9). Several chemical species have been implicated for NPF in the terrestrial troposphere, including sulfuric acid (H2SO4), base molecules [ammonia (NH3) and amines], oxidized organics, and ion clusters, along with environmental factors such as temperature, relative humidity (RH), solar radiation, and preexisting particles (10–19). Currently, many results from experimental, field, and theoretical studies of NPF are in conflict, especially with respect to the identities of the species contributing to the initial stage of aerosol formation (11, 19, 20). To date, there have been no direct measurements of the chemical constituents for particles smaller than about 8 nm (21), and consistent theories have yet to be established to account for NPF under different atmospheric conditions (11, 19).

Climate change alters emissions and atmospheric chemistry, inevitably affecting the gas-to-particle conversion and aerosol properties (1). The most recent decade (2015–2024) shows the highest average temperature, with a notable trend of increasing heat waves (22), and 2024 is the hottest year on record, with the average global temperature for the first time exceeding its preindustrial level by 1.5°C. NPF is believed to be favored at low or moderate temperatures (<20°C) because of decreased volatility for the condensing species (23, 24). For example, a series of recent studies suggested NPF from inorganic acids and NH3 as well as isoprene oxidation products at low temperatures characteristic of the upper troposphere (25–28). Conversely, limited field studies have been conducted to observe NPF at temperatures of >30°C (29, 30). In this work, we present field observations and quantum chemical calculations to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms relevant to the formation and growth of nanoparticles.

## Unprecedented NPF events

We conducted a comprehensive field study to assess atmospheric chemistry during a heat wave (“AC-HEAT”) in central Texas (fig. S1) by deploying a suite of state-of-the-art instruments to measure trace gases and nanoparticles (see supplementary materials). NPF was delineated by a sudden burst of sub-10-nm particles and their subsequent growth measured by a nano-differential mobility analyzer (NDMA) and an ultrafine condensation particle counter (UCPC) (Fig. 1 and fig. S2). In this work, we defined an NPF event as satisfying the following two conditions: (i) apparent formation and growth of sub-10-nm particles and (ii) the concentration of 3- to 25-nm particles (N3–25 commonly referred to as the nucleation mode) exceeded a value of 6000 cm−3. The event and nonevent days were differentiated by whether there existed a clear NPF event (Fig. 1 and figs. S2 and S3). The NPF event days occurred regularly during our AC-HEAT campaign, with a frequency of 56% (15 event days out of 27 days; table S1). Several distinctive features of aerosol formation and growth emerged from our measurements. During the event days, an initial NPF occurred consistently after sunrise at around 7:20 central daylight time (CDT), and there often existed multiple NPF occurrences. The concentration of nucleation-mode particles varied on event days (Fig. 1, D to F, and fig. S2), with the highest value reaching >20,000 cm−3 (Fig. 1D). The strongest NPF (with the largest N3–25) took place at different daytime hours on event days, when the particle size increased from 3 nm to 50 nm within 6 to 12 hours (Fig. 1, A to C, and fig. S2). The continuous increase in the particle size indicated that NPF occurred on a regional scale, whereas the discontinuity in the size growth curve was attributable to wind variations (fig. S4).

Previous field studies have identified two common NPF types: (i) instantaneous formation and rapid growth of nanoparticles characterized by a banana-shaped curve and (ii) continuous formation but slow growth of nanoparticles known as continuum-NPF (16). Most NPF events observed in this work closely resembled the latter type (Fig. 1, A to C, and fig. S2). Although elevated concentrations of nucleation-mode particles also existed on nonevent days (fig. S3), the formation and growth for sub-10-nm particles were less obvious. Indeed, NPF might still occur on nonevent days, as previously categorized by “quiet NPF” owing to the low sensitivity of NDMA and UCPC in the sub-10-nm range (31). For the three strongest NPF events (marked by the gray shading in Fig. 1), the average temperature and RH were 32° ± 3°C and 54 ± 10%, respectively (fig. S5). Notably, one NPF event occurred at an average temperature of 34°C (Fig. 1, B and H), and another appeared at an average temperature of 38°C (figs. S2I and S6). Such unusual NPF events at high temperatures approaching 40°C have not been previously recognized.

## Molecular-level characterization of nanoparticles

To remedy the gap for the lack of chemical speciation, we carried out measurements of size-resolved compositions of nanoparticles down to 3 nm using thermal desorption–ion drift–chemical ionization mass spectrometry (TD-ID-CIMS; fig. S7) (32–34). Briefly, ambient particles were size-selected by an NDMA, and the resultant monodisperse particles were then deposited on an electrostatic particle collector. Subsequently, thermally desorbed gases from the collected mass were analyzed using negative (CO3− and CO4− sensitive to acids by deprotonation) and positive (H3O+ sensitive to organics and amines by protonation) reagent ions. In total, we conducted 24 measurements for chemical compositions in the size range of 3 to 50 nm (table S2). Calibration for the TD-ID-CIMS yielded a detection limit of 0.01 to 0.06 ng (table S3 and fig. S8). The continuum-NPF in our fieldwork allowed for the collection of a sufficient particle mass during an extended period, which was essential for analyzing sub-10-nm particles.

We initially analyzed the chemical compositions for the smallest particles (3, 5, and 10 nm) using the negative reagent ions (Fig. 1, J to L). During the continuum-NPF, monodisperse particles were collected for ~3 hours, and the desorption area for each mass peak was integrated to derive the total collected mass, with the values of 0.5, 0.7, and 5.1 ng for 3-, 5-, and 10-nm particles, respectively. Alternatively, we estimated the deposited particle mass according to the collection time, the measured number concentration, and the particle collection efficiency, yielding 0.3, 0.6, and 4.6 ng for 3-, 5-, and 10-nm particles, respectively. A comparison between the two derived masses showed an agreement at 5 and 10 nm (within 86 to 90%) but a disparity (within 60%) at 3 nm: The former indicated an important mass closure in the composition measurements, whereas the latter was attributable to the lowest sensitivity of NDMA and UCPC for the smallest size. The observed mass closure for 5- and 10-nm particles implied that the TD-ID-CIMS measurements accounted for most of the species collected. For 3- to 10-nm particles, the species detected were predominantly organic acids consisting of one to three carboxylic groups (i.e., mono-, di-, and triacids; tables S4 and S5). The most abundant compounds included diacids such as glutaric acid [GlA, mass/charge ratio (m/z) = 131], adipic acid (AdA, m/z = 145), tartaric acid (TaA, m/z = 149), oxalic acid (OxA, m/z = 89), azelaic acid (AzA, m/z = 187), succinic acid (SuA, m/z = 117), pinic acid (PinA, m/z = 185), and phthalic acid (PhA, m/z = 165), followed by monoacids such as benzoic acid (BeA, m/z = 121), pyruvic acid (PyA, m/z = 87), 2-methylglyceric acid (MgA, m/z = 119), and toluic acid (ToA, m/z = 135) as well as triacids such as tricarballylic acid (TrA, m/z = 175) and citric acid (CiA, m/z = 191) (Fig. 1, J to L, and tables S4 and S5). We also found the presence of H2SO4 (m/z = 97) on 3- to 10-nm particles, although its signal was small. Additional measurements for 3- to 50-nm particles using the negative reagent ions are presented in Fig. 2, A to F, and all results for the identified species and their mass fractions are summarized in table S5. Collectively, the mass fractions of 3- to 10-nm particles were measured as 58 to 74% diacids, 15 to 24% monoacids, 6 to 14% triacids, and 2 to 4% H2SO4. The chemical composition and mass fraction at 20 nm were comparable to those at 3 to 10 nm. The mass fraction of H2SO4 increased noticeably with size, reaching 11% at 30 nm and 15% at 50 nm. In addition to the carboxylic functional group, several detected organic acids contained one (CiA) or two (MgA and TaA) hydroxyl groups and one carbonyl group (tables S4 and S5).

We also measured the chemical compositions of 5- to 50-nm particles using the positive reagent ions (Fig. 2, G to K, and table S6). The identified species for 5- and 10-nm particles were exclusively diacids (including GlA, TaA, AdA, SuA, OxA, PhA, and AzA), monoacids [BeA, MgA, PyA, and pinonic acid (PiA)], and triacids (including TrA and CiA) with comparable mass fractions (71 to 83% diacids, 13 to 20% monoacids, and 4 to 9% triacids) to those measured using the negative ion. Crucially, the consistency between the negative and positive reagent ions provides the unambiguous verification that multifunctional organic acids represent the dominant constituents for sub-10-nm particles (tables S5 and S6). On the other hand, a pronounced difference was observed in the chemical compositions between the smaller (5 to 10 nm) and larger (20 to 50 nm) particles. The measured mass fractions of diacids were much smaller for 20- to 50-nm particles (40 to 45%) than 5- to 10-nm particles (71 to 83%). We did not detect amines for particles smaller than 20 nm. Dimethylamine (m/z = 46) was identified for 30- and 50-nm particles, with mass fractions of 6 and 9%, respectively (Fig. 2, J and K, and table S6). Monomethylamine (m/z = 32) existed for 50-nm particles with a small mass fraction (1%). In addition, we detected several nonacidic organics (without the carboxylic functional group) for 20- to 50-nm particles. The mass fraction of the nonacidic organics increased with size, with mass fractions of 14, 15, and 24% for 20-, 30-, and 50-nm particles, respectively (Fig. 2, I to K, and table S6). The identified nonacidic organics included dihydroxyl toluene, isoprene-epoxydiol (IEPOX) or 4-hydroxyl-3-methyl-2-butenal, dimethylmaleic anhydride, nitrogen-containing organics (NCOs), and dimers and trimers for glyoxal, methylglyoxal, and hydroxyacetone. Several of the nonacidic organics, including NCOs and oligomeric products (dimers and trimers), were formed from heterogeneous reactions involving protonation and nucleophilic addition (35–37). The occurrence of aqueous reactions in larger particles, but not in smaller particles, indicated a distinction in the phase state (i.e., nondeliquescent versus deliquescent) that is relevant to the increasing amounts of H2SO4 and base species.

Size-resolved hygroscopicity and density of 5- to 50-nm particles were also investigated (Fig. 3). Except for the smallest size (5 nm), the hygroscopicity increased monotonically with size. For example, the hygroscopic growth factor (HGF) measured at 90% RH was 1.14 at 10 nm and increased to 1.53 at 50 nm (Fig. 3A). Previous experimental studies determined an HGF of 1.25 for GlA and 1.39 for TaA at 90% RH (table S4), higher than our values for 5- to 20-nm particles. Similarly, the measured density was low for 10- to 30-nm particles and increased for 50-nm particles, with corresponding values of 1.23 to 1.25 g cm−3 and 1.33 g cm−3, respectively (Fig. 3B). The densities for pure organic acids vary with their structures (table S4): The values are 1.43 g cm−3 for GlA and 1.79 g cm−3 for TaA, much higher than those measured for 10- to 30-nm particles. As elaborated below, the increase in HGF and density with particle size is likely linked to changes in chemical composition and phase state. In particular, the low hygroscopicity and density of nucleation-mode particles exemplify the distinctive characteristics of organics-rich nanostructures. In addition, the hygroscopicity of aerosolized nanodroplets also exhibits a pronounced size dependence (38).

Organic acids have been recognized as the common products from photooxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) of biogenic origin (e.g., isoprene and pinenes) and anthropogenic (e.g., aromatics) origin (36, 37, 39, 40) and one of the abundant constituents for secondary organic aerosols (40, 41). For example, environmental chamber experiments of hydroxyl radical (OH)–initiated oxidation have identified MgA and PyA from isoprene; GlA, SuA, OxA, BeA, and ToA from aromatics (toluene and m-xylene); and PiA and PinA from pinenes (36, 37, 39, 40), which were detected for nucleation-mode particles in our study. Also, we detected two fatty acids in nanoparticles (palmitic and stearic acids with small mass fractions; tables S5 and S6), which are known molecular markers in cooking emissions (42). All identified nonacidic organics have been previously reported as the major particle-phase components of OH-initiated oxidation of isoprene and aromatics (36, 37, 43).

## Atmospheric conditions during NPF

To establish the sources for the NPF gaseous precursors, we measured the ambient concentrations of VOCs and their oxidation products using a high-resolution proton transfer reaction–time-of-flight mass spectrometer (HR-PTR-ToF-MS) (tables S7 and S8). We compared the temporal variations of total aromatics (i.e., the sum of toluene, xylenes, trimethylbenzene, and benzene), isoprene, and pinenes (Fig. 4, A to C) for the three NPF event days in Fig. 1. Isoprene and aromatics were the most abundant VOC types, with comparable concentrations of 1 to 4 parts per billion (ppb), and the pinene concentration ranged from 0.07 to 0.7 ppb. The concentration of total aromatics exhibited a clear morning peak and a weak evening peak, indicative of traffic-related emissions (6). In addition, we detected various gaseous organic acids, including GlA, PyA, PiA, MgA, AdA, ToA, and SuA (Fig. 4, D to F, and fig. S9) that were present in nucleation-mode particles (Figs. 1 and 2 and tables S5 and 6). Most organic acids measured in the gas phase showed a large increase during the daytime, consistent with their photochemical origins from VOC oxidation. GlA, MgA, PyA, and PiA were the most abundant organic acids measured in the gas phase (Fig. 4 and fig. S9), attributable to aromatic, isoprene, and pinene oxidation (36, 37, 39–41). All gaseous organic acids detected in our study were volatile or semivolatile, and their measured concentrations were much lower than their corresponding saturation vapor pressures (table S4), indicating that volatility-based equilibrium partitioning cannot explain our observed NPF. Throughout our fieldwork, we measured a negligible concentration for sulfur dioxide (SO2), with an estimated upper limit of ~0.5 ppb. The low SO2 level was responsible for the trace amount of H2SO4 detected in nucleation-mode particles (3 to 20 nm). For the three strong NPF events in Fig. 1, the average concentrations of O3, NOx (NO + NO2), and PM2.5 (particulate matter smaller than 2.5 μm) were 37 ± 8 ppb, 1.3 ± 0.5 ppb, and 7 ± 3 μg m−3 (Fig. 4G and fig. S10), respectively, corresponding to clean conditions (5, 6). In particular, the small concentration of PM2.5 reflected a low level of preexisting particles and a minimal condensation sink (CS; defined in eq. S10), which is favorable for NPF (fig. S11). Also, the low NOx level (with an average value of 1.3 ppb) indicated negligible formation of organic nitrates, which were undetected in both the gas and particle phases during our fieldwork. Furthermore, the measured solar irradiance was 640 ± 60 W m−2, indicating strong radiation during the NPF events. The high VOC emissions and intense solar radiation during the heat wave enhanced photochemical processes to effectively promote VOC oxidation and produce organic acids, facilitating the formation and growth of nucleation-mode particles. Moreover, most of the nonevent days corresponded to cloudy conditions (table S1), because of reduced solar radiation. Notably, NPF was rarely observed over the weekend during our field campaign, due to decreased aromatic concentrations from traffic emissions and cloudy conditions (table S1).

We derived the formation and growth rates from the measured concentrations and size increase for nucleation-mode particles (FR3–25 in eq. S7 and GR3–25 in eq. S9, respectively). The average FR3–25 value during our field campaign was 1.3 ± 0.7 cm−3 s−1, lower than average values previously reported for urban (2.9 cm−3 s−1) and remote or rural sites (4.1 cm−3 s−1) (9). The FR3–25 value exhibited a correlation with the measured total concentration of gaseous organic acids, [OA] (coefficient of determination, R2 = 0.58) and the peak concentration of total aromatics in the morning (R2 = 0.86) (Fig. 4, H and I). In contrast, there was little correlation of FR3–25 with temperature from 24° to 39°C (R2 = 0.06) (fig. S11). Notably, the NPF events with the two highest FR3–25 values of 2.8 and 2.2 cm−3 s−1 occurred at the average temperatures of 31° and 38°C, respectively (Fig. 1A and fig. S2I). The measured GR3–25 was 4.2 ± 1.8 nm hour−1, comparable to the median values reported for urban (5.9 nm hour−1) and remote or rural (3.5 nm hour−1) locations (9).

Our observation site is surrounded by extensive oak forest and is adjacent to pine forest to the east (fig. S1, C and D), with major isoprene and pinene emissions, respectively. Also, this location lies at the center of the “Texas Triangle” megaregion (fig. S1B), an area influenced by regional anthropogenic emissions and experiencing a growing frequency of summertime heat waves. Back-trajectory analysis was performed to evaluate the impacts of regional transport. During our field campaign, the wind was mainly southeasterly, from the coastal region, 6 to 12 hours before NPF (fig. S12). For example, the air masses for two NPF events in Fig. 1 originated from Houston, a metropolitan center with major industrial facilities for anthropogenic VOCs, NOx, and SO2 emissions (6). Given that the size growth from 3 to 50 nm typically took 6 to 12 hours (Fig. 1, A to C), the increasing level of H2SO4 detected in larger particles (30 and 50 nm) (Figs. 1 and 2 and table S5) revealed a regional influence. Atmospheric soundings displayed variable heights of the planetary boundary layer (PBL): a lower PBL of 70 to 100 m in the morning and a higher PBL of ~1500 m in the afternoon (fig. S13), affecting the vertical mixing of gases and aerosols as well as their temporal variations (Figs. 1 and 4). Additionally, these atmospheric profiles suggested that vertical transport of nucleation-mode particles from the upper troposphere was implausible.

## Spontaneous NPF from hydrogen-bonded molecular self-assembly

In essence, the initial stage of NPF follows a stepwise, reversible kinetic process to produce a molecular aggregate, Ai (10) … A i - 1 ⇄ + M i - 1 - M i - 1 A i ⇄ + M i - M i A i + 1 … where M denotes a monomer to be added or removed, and i corresponds to the aggregation step or size. Using quantum chemical calculations, we simulated Ai formation with i = 2 to 6 (Fig. 5A). We first constructed a dimer between GlA and ToA (A2) and then consecutively added MgA, H2SO4, AzA, and TrA to produce A3 to A6, respectively. The GlA•ToA dimer consists of double hydrogen bonds with lengths of 1.64 and 1.65 Å and a Gibbs energy change (ΔG) of about −7.7 kcal mol−1. The ΔG value decreases successively with increasing size and reaches an overall value of −34.7 kcal mol−1 at 1.50 nm for A6 (Fig. 5B and table S9). Organic acids readily engage in hydrogen bond interaction with the carboxylic group acting both as a donor and a receptor (44), and H2SO4 behaves analogously as a diacid. For example, monomeric addition to produce A2 to A6 involves the formation of two hydrogen bonds with a ΔG value of −5.7 to −7.8 kcal mol−1, and the newly formed aggregate contains two to five vacant sites for further hydrogen-bond interactions. Molecular aggregation of organic acids is driven by dipole-dipole interactions and electrostatic attraction between the electronegative oxygen atom and electropositive hydrogen atom among the carboxylic groups (marked by the red arrows in Fig. 5A). At each step, the competition between the forward and backward reactions depends on the relative importance between the association (related to the product of the monomer concentration and the association rate constant) and decomposition (related to the stability or ΔG of the aggregate) rates. We calculated the dipole-dipole capture rate constant (kD defined in eq. S14) leading to A2 to A6 using the average temperature of 32°C from our fieldwork (fig. S5). The calculated kD ranges from 2.4 × 10−10 to 5.7 × 10−10 cm3 s−1 (table S9), indicating a kinetically favorable process even at high temperatures (Fig. 5C). The dipole-dipole capture rate constant exhibits a weak dependence on temperature (eq. S14). Also, because of the large size and many degrees of vibrational modes for Ai, the temperature effect on the hydrogen bond strength is expected to be minimal. We further assessed GR3–25 using the average kD value for A2 to A6 and the measured total concentrations of organic acids during the NPF events (eq. S12). The predicted GR3–25 is a factor of 5 to 11 larger than those derived from the measured size increase (Fig. 4I and fig. S14), implying that only a small portion of the dipole-induced collisions contributes to the growth of nucleation-mode particles. Such an observation is explainable by evaporation of simple organic acids during aggregation, especially for monoacids (such as PyA, PiA, and MgA), as evidenced by small mass fractions (tables S5 and S6) measured in nucleation-mode particles but high abundance measured in the gas phase (Fig. 4, D to F, and fig. S9).

To gain a mechanistic insight into the observed NPF events, we conceptualized a kinetic pathway through molecular self-assembly to yield supramolecular nanoparticles (Fig. 5D). This phenomenon arises from the spontaneous association of molecules to form large, complex nanostructures, which is facilitated by noncovalent interactions (45, 46). We optimized three nanostructures consisting of 20 to 60 diacids, monoacids, and triacids, along with trace H2SO4, in accordance with our measured chemical compositions (tables S5 and S6). Molecular aggregation of organic acids is contingent on the intermolecular forces and proceeds spontaneously because of a continuing ΔG decrease with hydrogen-bond formation (Fig. 5B and table S9). Specifically, the molecular self-assembly is kinetically driven by the interplay of the dipole-dipole interaction and electrostatic attraction among the carboxylic groups (as illustrated by the red arrows in Fig. 5A). Another criterion for the molecular self-assembly lies in the availability of vacant sites for hydrogen-bond formation. Ideally, multifunction organic acids such as diacids and triacids as well as those with the hydroxyl and carbonyl groups are mostly preferred, as they offer multiple branches for growth and stabilization. Monoacids also contribute to the size increase but are prone to evaporation because of no further stabilization. Although a base molecule (NH3 or amines) forms a strong hydrogen-bonded pair with organic acid (or H2SO4), their association merely depletes the reactive sites and does not elongate the aggregate. Those notions are substantiated by the observations that diacids exhibit the largest mass fractions detected in nucleation-mode particles (Figs. 1 and 2 and tables S5 and S6) as well as their high abundance measured in the gas phase (Fig. 4, D to F). We conclude that self-assembly of multifunctional organic acids is responsible for the formation and growth of nucleation-mode particles in our field measurements (Fig. 1 and fig. S2).

An examination of the supramolecular nanostructures reveals several intrinsic features (Fig. 5D). The equivalent particle size increases from 2.0 nm to 2.9 nm for 20 to 60 molecules, respectively; the latter is detectable by NDMA, UCPC, and TD-ID-CIMS. Except for the carboxylic, hydroxyl, and carbonyl sites, the main backbone of organic acids is hydrophobic. Also, it is evident in Fig. 5 that those nanostructures correspond to a nondeliquescent state. In addition, the supramolecular nanoparticles connected by noncovalent hydrogen bonds contain various spacious open cavities. On the basis of the optimized structures, we estimated a density of ~1.1 g cm−3 for the three nanoparticles. These characteristics are consistent with the low hygroscopicity and density of nucleation-mode particles observed in our fieldwork (Fig. 3). The increasing amounts of H2SO4 and base molecules (amines) enable the conversion from a nondeliquescent to a deliquescent state and elevate the particle hygroscopicity and density for larger particles (Fig. 3). Under such circumstances, base molecules effectively stabilize organic acids as well as H2SO4 through the formation of aminium salts, promoting heterogeneous chemistry to produce the nonacidic organics.

## Conclusions

For nearly a century, homogeneous particle formation from vapors has been thought to occur in a two-step process involving a free energy barrier (nonspontaneous) and a curvature barrier (volatility-limited) (20, 47). An unexpected outcome from our field observations is the high temperatures (approaching 40°C) at which frequent NPF events take place. Such a finding cannot be explained by presently known theories for NPF, especially in terms of thermodynamics-driven nucleation dependent on volatility. By contrast, our work has unfolded a spontaneous NPF mechanism to produce supramolecular nanoparticles through hydrogen-bonded molecular self-assembly, which corroborates the field observations of frequent NPF events during the heat wave. The revelation of the chemical identity of nanoparticles down to 3 nm provides the first definitive evidence that multifunctional organic acids (especially diacids) contribute dominantly to the formation of nucleation-mode particles. Detection of gaseous organic acids in the atmosphere confirms their critical role in NPF as well as their origins from photooxidation of anthropogenic and biogenic emissions, such as traffic-related aromatics and biogenic-related isoprene and pinenes, respectively. The organics-rich nanoparticles exhibit distinct physicochemical properties, notably with low hygroscopicity and density (about 1.2 g cm−3). Given that organic acids are ubiquitously produced from photooxidation of anthropogenic and biogenic VOCs (36, 37, 39), their self-assembly (along with H2SO4) to produce hydrogen-bonded supramolecular nanoparticles represents a common mechanism for NPF under diverse tropospheric conditions.

The implications of this work are far-reaching. A critical aspect in climate projection arises from varying anthropogenic and biogenic emissions. For example, large emission shifts are anticipated from the preindustrial era (with only biogenic emissions), to the present (with both biogenic and anthropogenic emissions), to the future (with dominant biogenic emissions and reduced anthropogenic emissions under a warm climate) (1). Our measurements conducted at high temperatures and with high biogenic emissions (isoprene and pinenes) but minor industrial influences (low SO2 and NOx) offer fresh perspectives on the chemistry-climate interaction. Specifically, the future scenario under global warming likely promotes NPF because of high biogenic (especially pinenes) emissions and strong solar radiation. On the other hand, the observed low aerosol mass concentration (typically <10 μg m−3) and inefficient cloud-forming potential (low hygroscopicity) of the organic-dominant nanoparticles hamper the aerosol-radiation and aerosol-cloud interactions, indicating positive feedback on heat waves and global warming. As the deadliest among hazard weather events, extreme heat triggers a variety of stress conditions to cause human fatality (48). Also, NPF represents an important source of ultrafine particles (<50 nm, as shown in Fig. 1 and fig. S2), which induce strong adverse human health effects because of their ability to enter extrapulmonary tissues, especially in vulnerable individuals such as children and pregnant women (49, 50). The toxicity of ultrafine particles is linked to their chemical makeup and properties, and the particle acidity induces oxidative stress and inflammation (51). Our results suggest plausible compound health risks from coexposure to extreme heat and acidic ultrafine particles. Moreover, although molecular self-assembly through noncovalent interactions in the condensed phase has emerged as an important synthetic strategy to produce nanomaterials with distinct functions (45, 46), few studies have explored such a pathway from the gas phase. The discovery of aerosol formation by hydrogen-bonded molecular self-assembly represents the first attempt to characterize supramolecular nanoparticles by integrating advanced instruments to measure their chemical composition and physicochemical properties. Hence, this work not only opens the potential for reliably assessing the impacts of atmospheric aerosols on public health, cloud formation, and climate, but also has broader implications for many biological, chemical, engineering, medical, and physical disciplines.
